title: After the ruins came a Book of light.
subtitle: Guidance given so people would remember

row.title: rules to follow
sub: a list of dos and don'ts

then: After Fir'awn and his chiefs were destroyed, Allah revealed {reward}the Tawrah to Musa{/reward}. Ibn Kathir explains it as guidance out of blindness and error, and {idea}a mercy that shows the way to righteous deeds{/idea}, so that people would be reminded.
now: You have been through a hard year: a breakup, a job loss, a scare. Afterwards, what you need is not more noise but {idea}a clear light to walk by{/idea}. That is what Allah gives after the ruins.
old: Scripture is mostly rules and warnings.
new: Allah's Book is light and mercy, given so I can see where to walk and remember Him.
try: Read a short passage of the Quran today looking only for one thing that gives you light.

title: You were not there, yet you told it exactly.
subtitle: How the Prophet ﷺ knew Musa's story

row.title: revelation
sub: as if hearing and seeing it

then: Having told Musa's story from start to end, Allah reminds the Prophet ﷺ that he {idea}was not on the western side of the mount{/idea}. Ibn Kathir notes he could not read books and grew up among people who knew nothing of this. Similar lines come after the stories of Maryam and Nuh.
now: You have just read the whole story of Musa in this surah, detail after detail. {idea}Pause on who delivered it{/idea}: a man in Makkah who never sat with historians, telling it as if he had been there.
old: The Quran's stories are just retellings of older ones.
new: The Prophet ﷺ told these events as an eyewitness would, and that itself points to Allah as their source.
try: Think of one detail from Musa's story that moved you, and say a salawat on the Prophet ﷺ who brought it.

title: Long ages passed, so Allah kept sending messengers.
subtitle: Why reminders are needed again
then: Ibn Kathir explains that {trap}people had forgotten the evidence{/trap} Allah established through earlier Prophets. The Prophet ﷺ never lived among the people of Madyan reciting to them, yet told of Shu'ayb. {idea}It is Allah who kept sending.{/idea}
now: You came back from Hajj or Ramadan glowing. Six months later, the glow is gone and old habits are back. {idea}Forgetting over time is human.{/idea} That is why Allah keeps sending reminders, and why you need to keep returning to them.
old: I learned this once, so I do not need reminding.
new: Long stretches of time wear down memory, so I need Allah's reminders again and again.
try: Set one weekly reminder on your phone to read a short surah you already know.

title: Not a witness at the mount, but sent as mercy.
subtitle: A warner for a people who had none
then: Qatadah said the call at Tur refers to Allah calling Musa. The Prophet ﷺ was not there, but Allah revealed it to him {reward}as a mercy to him and to His servants{/reward}, sent to Arabs who {idea}had no warner before him{/idea}.
now: A friend texts you, "Are you sure about this?" before you sign the loan. It annoys you. Later you realise it saved you. {reward}A warning from someone who cares is a mercy.{/reward}
old: Warnings are a burden and a downer.
new: Allah sending a warner is itself a mercy, so I would not walk into harm unaware.
try: Thank one person this week who once warned you away from a mistake.

title: So no one could say: nobody ever told us.
subtitle: Removing the last excuse
then: Ibn Kathir explains that the Prophet ﷺ was sent {idea}to establish proof and leave no excuse{/idea}, so that no one could say no warner ever came. He links it to {idea}"so that mankind should have no plea against Allah after the Messengers"{/idea}.
now: You know the Quran is on the shelf. You know the app is on your phone. {idea}"No one ever told me" is not really available to you anymore.{/idea} That is not a threat. It is an invitation that has already arrived.
old: If I never really looked into it, I cannot be blamed.
new: The message has already reached me, so the question now is what I do with it.
try: Open the Quran today and read one passage you have never read before.

title: Give us Musa's miracles, they said, then rejected those too.
subtitle: When no amount of proof is enough
then: When truth came, the Makkans asked {trap}why he was not given what Musa was given{/trap}: the staff, the hand, the parting sea. Yet Fir'awn saw all of that and still denied. Then they called both {trap}"two works of magic supporting each other"{/trap} and rejected them together.
now: You tell yourself you will start praying once you understand everything. Then you understand, and you need one more answer. {trap}The goalpost keeps moving.{/trap} Notice when a question is really a delay.
old: I will believe properly once I get the right sign.
new: If every proof gets a new excuse, the problem is not the proof.
try: Name one excuse you keep giving for a good habit. Do the habit once today anyway.

title: Bring a better guide, and I will follow it.
subtitle: An open challenge to the doubters
then: Ibn Abbas said the "two" here are {idea}the Tawrah and the Quran{/idea}, which Allah often mentions together. The Prophet ﷺ was told to answer: then {idea}bring a Book from Allah that guides better{/idea}, and I will follow it.
now: Your friend mocks your faith at dinner. Fair enough, you might say: what do you live by that guides you better? {idea}Criticism is easy. Offering a better path is harder.{/idea}
old: If people criticise my faith, I have to win every point.
new: I can calmly ask what better guidance they have to offer.
try: Write down three ways the Quran has guided a decision of yours. Keep the list.

title: No answer means they only follow their desires.
subtitle: The real reason behind refusing
then: If they could not answer, Ibn Kathir says, it showed they {trap}follow their own desires with no basis or evidence{/trap}. The verse asks: who is more astray than one who follows desire {idea}without guidance from Allah{/idea}?
now: You decide to skip the hard conversation, then find reasons it is the wise choice. You want the thing, then build the argument. {trap}Desire first, logic afterwards.{/trap} Notice the order in your own head.
old: My choices are based on careful reasoning.
new: Often I follow what I want and dress it up as reasoning, unless I check it against Allah's guidance.
try: Before one decision today, ask: is this what I want, or what is right? Answer honestly.

title: Word after word, so they might remember.
subtitle: A message conveyed piece by piece
then: Mujahid said this means {idea}"We have explained the Word to them"{/idea}, and that it was addressed to Quraysh. Qatadah said Allah told them what He did in the past and what He will do in the future, {reward}that they might remember{/reward}.
now: Your mother has told you the same thing a hundred times: call your grandmother. One day it finally lands. {idea}Repeated reminders are a sign someone has not given up on you.{/idea}
old: If I have heard a reminder before, it has nothing new for me.
new: Allah repeats His message out of care, waiting for the day it sinks in.
try: Pick one reminder you have heard many times and act on it once today.

title: Those who knew the earlier Book recognised this one.
subtitle: People who heard the Quran and believed
then: Sa'id bin Jubayr said this was revealed about seventy priests sent by An-Najashi. The Prophet ﷺ recited Surah Ya Sin to them; {reward}they began to weep and embraced Islam{/reward}.
now: You have studied something deeply, and then someone shows you a truth that fits what you already know. {idea}Real knowledge makes you quicker to recognise truth, not slower.{/idea} Let what you know make you humble, not defensive.
old: The more I know, the harder it is for anyone to teach me.
new: Sincere knowledge prepares the heart to recognise truth when it arrives.
try: Listen to someone today with the aim of learning one thing, not of correcting them.

title: We were already submitting before it came.
subtitle: When a new truth completes an old faith
then: When the Quran was recited to them they said {idea}"It is the truth from our Lord."{/idea} Ibn Kathir explains their words: even before it came, {reward}they believed in One God and responded sincerely to His commands{/reward}.
now: You grew up praying, but only now do you understand what you say. It is not a new religion; {idea}it is the same submission, finally seen clearly{/idea}. Every return to Allah builds on what came before.
old: Growing in faith means my past practice did not count.
new: Sincere submission before now is what makes it easy to say yes when the truth becomes clear.
try: Thank Allah for one good habit you learned as a child that still holds you today.

title: Double reward for patience and answering evil with good.
subtitle: Three habits that earn twice
then: Ibn Kathir explains they are patient because {idea}holding to the truth is not easy{/idea}. He cites the hadith in the Sahih that three are given their reward twice, including a person of the Book who believed in his Prophet and then in Muhammad ﷺ. They {reward}repel evil with good{/reward}.
now: A colleague takes credit for your work in the meeting. Your sibling says something cutting at Eid. You could hit back. {reward}Or you could answer with a good word and move on.{/reward} That choice is what the verse rewards.
old: If someone wrongs me, a fair response is to wrong them back.
new: Answering wrong with good, patiently, is what earns a double reward.
try: Next time someone is unkind to you today, reply with one genuinely kind sentence.

title: Peace be upon you. We are not here to argue.
subtitle: Walking away from ugly talk with dignity
then: When foolish people spoke to them foolishly, Ibn Kathir says, {idea}they turned away and did not respond in kind{/idea}. They said: to us our deeds, to you yours, peace be upon you. He links it to passing by vain talk {reward}with dignity{/reward}.
now: The comments under your post turn nasty. The uncle at the wedding starts in on you again. {idea}You can say "peace be with you" and leave the thread.{/idea} Not every insult needs your reply.
old: If I do not answer back, I look weak.
new: Walking away from ugly talk with a word of peace is strength, not weakness.
try: Leave one argument today, online or offline, with a calm word and no reply after it.

title: You cannot guide even those you love most.
subtitle: Guidance belongs to Allah alone
then: Recorded in the Two Sahihs: this was revealed about Abu Talib, the Prophet's ﷺ uncle who protected and loved him. On his deathbed the Prophet ﷺ kept urging him to say La ilaha illallah, but {trap}he refused{/trap}. Allah told His Messenger ﷺ that {idea}guidance is not in your hands{/idea}.
now: Your father, your brother, your best friend from school. You have prayed and talked and hoped for years. {idea}Your part is to love them and convey it well.{/idea} The opening of a heart belongs to Allah, not to you.
old: If someone I love does not change, I have failed them.
new: Even the Prophet ﷺ could not guide his beloved uncle; my part is to convey, and Allah guides.
try: Make dua for one person you wish would come closer to Allah, and let go of the pressure.

title: Afraid of losing their safety, inside a safe sanctuary.
subtitle: The excuse that ignores where safety comes from
then: Some Makkans said that if they followed the guidance, {trap}the pagan tribes around them would attack{/trap}. Allah answered: did We not give them {reward}a secure sanctuary{/reward}, with fruits brought from Ta'if and beyond? It was safe while they worshipped idols; why not when they follow the truth?
now: You do not pray at work because your colleagues might think you strange and your career might stall. {idea}The job, the salary, the safe flat you live in already came from Allah.{/idea} He does not take away safety for obeying Him.
old: If I openly practise my faith, I will lose my security.
new: The safety I fear losing was given by Allah, who will not abandon me for following Him.
try: Do one small act of faith openly today that you usually hide out of worry.
